title: How to Stay Close to a Teenager Who Is Pulling Away
excerpt: A teenager pulling away is doing exactly what they are supposed to do. The work is to stay reachable without chasing, present without smothering.
body:
There is a particular grief in watching a child who once told you everything become a teenager who answers in one syllable. You feel the door closing and you want to force it. But the pulling away is not a malfunction. It is the work of becoming a separate person, and a teenager who never pulls away has a different and worse problem. The goal is not to stop the separation. It is to stay close through it, so that when they come back, and they do come back, the relationship is still there.

This season humbled me. The parenting moves that worked when they were small stopped working overnight, and I had to learn new ones in the dark.

## Stop interrogating, start being available

The instinct when a teenager goes quiet is to ask more questions. "How was your day? What happened? Why won't you talk to me?" Every question feels to them like a demand, and they answer with the silence that demands earn. The harder you pursue, the faster they retreat.

Try the opposite. Be present without prying. Drive them somewhere and say nothing. Sit in the kitchen while they eat and talk about nothing important. Teenagers open up sideways, on their own schedule, usually in a car or late at night, and almost never when summoned. Your job is to be reliably around and unthreatening, so that when the moment comes, you are there to catch it. The conversations you want cannot be scheduled. They can only be made possible.

## Respect the door they are closing

A teenager building a separate self needs you to honor the boundary, not breach it. Knock on the closed door. Ask before reading the diary. Give them privacy that is real, not surveillance dressed as trust. Yes, you watch for genuine danger, and there are limits to privacy when safety is on the line. But the daily texture should be respect, because a teenager who feels respected stays connected, and one who feels spied on disappears.

This is the hardest pivot for a parent who used to know everything. You are moving from manager to consultant, from someone who runs their life to someone they might choose to ask. The authority you cling to, you lose. The trust you extend, you tend to get back.

## Stay warm even when they are cold

The teenager will test whether your love depends on their affection. They will be sullen, dismissive, sometimes cruel, and watch to see if you withdraw. Do not. Stay warm in the face of cold. Keep saying good morning to the grunt. Keep saying I love you to the eye roll. Keep showing up to the game even when they act like they did not want you there.

This is the love the father shows in the parable, the one who keeps the porch light on and the heart open while the son is far off. Your steadiness is the fixed point they push against to find their shape. They need you to not move. "Love is patient," Paul writes, and the teen years are where that sentence gets tested down to the bone.

## Keep doing things shoulder to shoulder

Teenagers who will not talk face to face will often talk side by side. Find something to do together that is not a conversation. Cook. Drive. Throw a ball. Work on the car. Watch their show, the one you do not understand, and let them explain it. Connection in these years comes through shared activity more than through talking about feelings. Get next to them doing something, and the words come on their own.

## Keep the door open with your own steadiness

More than anything, a teenager needs to know that the way back is always open, no matter how far they have wandered or how badly a conversation went. Do not close the door from your side in a moment of hurt or anger. They may slam it from theirs a hundred times. You hold yours open. When they say something cruel, do not retaliate in kind, even when you want to. When they push you away, do not stay away. The pulling away is a test of whether your love is sturdy enough to outlast their need to separate, and your steadiness across these years is the answer. They are watching, even when they pretend not to, to see whether you will still be there when the storm of adolescence passes. Be there. That is the whole assignment.

## This week

Pick one day and ask your teenager nothing. Instead, be present and easy, available without an agenda. Then find one shoulder-to-shoulder thing, however small, and do it with them. When they are cold, stay warm anyway. You are proving across this whole season that the door is open from your side and always will be, and that when they are ready to walk back through it, you will be exactly where they left you.
